title: Static Allocation
body:
[[Variable]]s 

---

Memory decided at **compile time**. The compiler knows the type, so it knows the size, so it
can reserve the space before the program ever runs.

```c++
int x;              // 4 bytes, decided now
const int SIZE = 50;
int scores[SIZE];   // 200 bytes, decided now
```

Everything ordinary is statically allocated: locals, globals, fixed [[Array]]s, [[Structure]]s.
Locals live on the stack and come and go with the block; see [[Stack and Heap]] and
[[Variable Lifetime]].

The limitation is the whole reason the next topic exists:

```c++
int n;
cin >> n;
int scores[n];      // compile error: n is not known at compile time
```

The size had to be a constant, and input arrives too late. That is what
[[Dynamic Allocation]] and [[new And delete]] are for, and it is the reason
[[Dynamic Arrays]] and every [[Linked Structure]] in the course are built out of [[Pointer]]s.

The trade is the usual one. Static is fast and cannot leak; dynamic is flexible and is yours
to clean up. Declaring `int scores[1000]` and using twelve of them is the bad middle ground
[[Dynamic Allocation]] complains about.
